dedupe_keys.name: projected national climate risk to the benefits of aquatic food systems fisheries and aquaculture 2030 2090

description: This data set rates, country by country, how much climate change threatens the food, nutrition, jobs and income that people get from fisheries and fish farming. The producers are Michelle Tigchelaar, Hanna Payne and Elizabeth Selig of Stanford University, William Cheung of the University of British Columbia, and Essam Mohammed and Michael Phillips of WorldFish. Their fuzzy logic model combines projected climate hazards to marine and freshwater capture fisheries and aquaculture with how much each country relies on aquatic foods and how vulnerable it is to losing them. Coverage is national, for a high and a low emissions scenario in three windows around 2030, 2050 and 2090. The results workbook and a detailed readme are available as a free download from Dryad and a Zenodo copy under a CC0 public domain dedication. Caveats: composite risk scores, not tonnes of food, national averages, and results depend on the underlying ocean and freshwater projections. Simulation uses: flagging countries whose food supply depends on climate-exposed fisheries, and weighting aquatic food losses in food security stress tests and adaptation planning. Related records: the global food security projections database (data-global-food-security-projections-database) covers overall food demand and hunger.
